title: Japanese Shojin Ryori Root Vegetable Stew
summary: Rooted in traditional Japanese temple cooking, this Shojin Ryori stew delivers pure plant-based comfort without relying on animal products. Built around a rich base of kombu and dashi, it showcases sweet daikon radish, taro root, and lotus root simmered gently in savory seasonings. Mirin and light soy sauce create a subtle balance between natural sweetness and umami depth. This nourishing vegetarian stew offers clean, grounding flavors that highlight seasonal earthy vegetables. Each bowl delivers gentle warmth, ideal for a quiet evening meal that satisfies without feeling heavy. High in fiber and loaded with natural minerals, it provides wholesome plant nutrients in a refined format. Taking time to trim and score the root vegetables allows them to absorb maximum broth while retaining their distinct structural textures during cooking. Serve hot with a sprinkle of shichimi togarashi for an authentic temple-style dining experience.

steps.step: Wipe the dried kombu kelp gently with a damp cloth to clean without removing white powder.
Place kombu and dried shiitake mushrooms into a glass jug containing one liter of water.
Steep the kelp and mushrooms at room temperature for thirty minutes to extract initial umami.
Pour the mixture into a medium saucepan and warm gently over low heat for fifteen minutes.
Remove the kombu kelp just before the water reaches a boil to prevent bitter flavors.
Strain the warm mushroom dashi through a fine sieve into a bowl, reserving the mushrooms.
Stem the softened shiitake caps and slice each cap into neat quarters for the stew base.
Measure out eight hundred milliliters of clean strained dashi broth for use in cooking.
Whisk white miso paste into fifty milliliters of warm dashi until completely smooth.
Set the rich vegetarian dashi broth aside while preparing all root vegetables next.
Peel the daikon radish and slice into thick rounds, rounding the sharp outer edges neatly.
Cut a shallow crisscross pattern on one side of each daikon round to aid cooking process.
Peel the satoimo taro roots, rub with sea salt, rinse thoroughly, and cut into bite-sized halves.
Peel the lotus root and slice into half-inch rounds, soaking immediately in vinegar water.
Scrape burdock root skin lightly with the back of a knife and shave into thin diagonals.
Cut carrots into decorative flower shapes or simple quarter-inch thick uniform diagonal coins.
Tear the konjac block into small irregular pieces using spoons for better texture retention.
Blanch konjac pieces in boiling water for two minutes to remove residual alkaline taste.
Pour hot boiling water over fried tofu puffs to drain off surface oil, then cut into halves.
String snow peas and blanch in salted water for thirty seconds until vibrant green color.
Heat sesame oil in a heavy pot over medium heat and sauté shaved burdock for two minutes.
Add daikon radish, lotus root, and carrots into the pot, tossing with burdock root evenly.
Pour in the reserved dashi broth, soy sauce, mirin, sake, and sugar, stirring to dissolve.
Bring liquid to a gentle simmer over medium heat, skimming any white foam from surface.
Add blanched konjac pieces, sliced shiitake caps, and prepared taro root into the simmering pot.
Cover pot with a wooden drop-lid to keep vegetables submerged in broth during simmering.
Simmer gently over low heat for twenty-five minutes until daikon turns translucent and soft.
Add fried tofu puffs and grated ginger into broth, simmering uncovered for five minutes.
Slurry potato starch with cold water and stir into stew to create a subtle light body.
Stir in the dissolved miso mixture right at the end without letting the broth boil further.
Turn off the burner and allow the stew to rest covered for ten minutes before serving guests.
Thinly slice green scallions on a sharp angle to create delicate fresh green garnishes.
Divide root vegetables, tofu puffs, and konjac evenly among four deep ceramic soup bowls.
Ladle warm savory dashi broth over the arranged vegetables in each bowl until filled.
Top each portion with blanched green snow peas for vibrant visual color contrast.
Garnish center with sliced scallions and a light sprinkle of toasted white sesame seeds.
Offer shichimi togarashi spice blend on the side for diners wanting additional heat.
Serve stew immediately alongside hot steamy Japanese short-grain rice and green tea.
Ensure every bowl contains balanced proportions of roots, broth, and bright green peas.
Refrigerate remaining stew in covered bowl; flavors enhance nicely when reheated tomorrow.
